questions.prompt: Each closed fermion loop in a diagram of the imaginary-time expansion contributes which factor?
questions.solution: Fermion loops give $(-1)^F$ (Eq. 13.18, rule 5). The spin sum over a loop is a separate factor 2. The $1/\beta$ factors come from the Matsubara sums over internal frequencies, not from the loop itself.

questions.prompt: Explain why disconnected diagrams drop out of $\mathcal G(b,a)$ in Eq. (13.7).
questions.solution: The numerator contains terms where the external vertices $a$ and $b$ connect to one piece, and other pieces are vacuum diagrams with no external line. The vacuum pieces are products of the same diagrams that appear in the denominator $\langle\hat U(\beta,0)\rangle_0$. The denominator divides out these products exactly, so only connected diagrams remain (Eqs. 13.15-13.17).

questions.prompt: Solve the Dyson equation $\mathcal G=\mathcal G_0+\mathcal G_0\Sigma\mathcal G$ in Fourier space for $\mathcal G$ in terms of $\Sigma$, with $\mathcal G_0(k,ik_n)=1/(ik_n-\xi_k)$.
questions.solution:
Write the equation as $\mathcal G^{-1}=\mathcal G_0^{-1}-\Sigma$. Then
$$\mathcal G(k,ik_n)=\frac{1}{\mathcal G_0^{-1}-\Sigma}=\frac{1}{ik_n-\xi_k-\Sigma(k,ik_n)}.$$

questions.prompt: In jellium with the Coulomb interaction, the Hartree self-energy is $W(0)N/\mathcal V$. What happens to it?
choices: It is cancelled by the positive background, which removes the $q=0$ term
It diverges and is not cancelled
questions.solution: The $q=0$ Hartree term is cancelled exactly by the uniform positive background of the jellium model (Eq. 2.34), so $\Sigma^H$ vanishes. The Fock term is momentum dependent, so the first two options describe the Fock term, not the Hartree term.

questions.prompt: Book Exercise 13.1. Evaluate the Matsubara sum $\frac1\beta\sum_{ip_n}\frac{e^{ip_n0^+}}{ip_n-\xi_p}$ with Eq. (11.57). Use it for the Fock self-energy $\Sigma^F_\sigma$ of Eq. (13.33) and the pair bubble $\Pi_0$ of Eq. (13.37), and check that the Hartree term gives $\Sigma^H_\sigma=W(0)N/\mathcal V$.
questions.solution:
1. By Eq. (11.57) with $g(z)=1/(z-\xi_p)$, the sum equals $n_F(\xi_p)$, as in ch11-H1. The factor $e^{ip_n0^+}$ is the same-time convergence factor of rule (6) in Eq. (13.27).
2. Fock (no fermion loop, $F=0$, internal spin fixed to $\sigma$, interaction line $-W(\mathbf k-\mathbf p)$): $\Sigma^F_\sigma(k)=-\int\frac{d\mathbf p}{(2\pi)^3}W(\mathbf k-\mathbf p)\,\frac1\beta\sum_{ip_n}\frac{e^{ip_n\eta}}{ip_n-\xi_p}=-\int\frac{d\mathbf p}{(2\pi)^3}W(\mathbf k-\mathbf p)\,n_F(\xi_p)$.
3. Hartree ($F=1$ gives $-1$, the interaction line gives $-W(0)$, the spin sum gives 2): $\Sigma^H_\sigma=2W(0)\int\frac{d\mathbf p}{(2\pi)^3}n_F(\xi_p)=W(0)N/\mathcal V$.
4. Pair bubble: with $F=1$ and spin sum 2, $\Pi_0(q,iq_n)=-2\int\frac{d\mathbf p}{(2\pi)^3}\frac1\beta\sum_{ip_n}\frac{1}{(ip_n+iq_n-\xi_{p+q})(ip_n-\xi_p)}$. The poles of $g(z)$ are $z=\xi_p$ and $z=\xi_{p+q}-iq_n$, and $n_F(\xi_{p+q}-iq_n)=n_F(\xi_{p+q})$ for bosonic $iq_n$. Eq. (11.57) gives
$$\Pi_0(q,iq_n)=-2\int\frac{d\mathbf p}{(2\pi)^3}\frac{n_F(\xi_p)-n_F(\xi_{p+q})}{iq_n+\xi_p-\xi_{p+q}}=-\chi_0(q,iq_n),$$
which is Eq. (14.21) up to the sign convention $\chi_0\equiv-\Pi_0$ of Eq. (14.12).

questions.prompt: Book Exercise 13.2. Expand the numerator and denominator of $\mathcal G(b,a)$ in Eq. (13.7) to second order in $W$. Show that the disconnected pieces cancel and that $\mathcal G=\mathcal G_0+\mathcal N_1^c+\mathcal N_2^c+O(W^3)$, where $\mathcal N^c_n$ are the connected $n$-th order contributions.
questions.solution:
Write the denominator as $D=1+D_1+D_2+\cdots$, where $D_n$ are the vacuum diagrams of order $n$ (Eq. 13.14). Every numerator diagram factorizes into a part connected to the external points $a$ and $b$ times a vacuum part (Eqs. 13.15-13.16). Summing all vacuum parts of every order gives the same series $D$, so
$$N=(\mathcal G_0+N_1^c+N_2^c+\cdots)\,(1+D_1+D_2+\cdots),$$
where $N^c_n$ is the connected $n$-th order contribution. Through second order,
$$N=\mathcal G_0(1+D_1+D_2)+N_1^c(1+D_1)+N_2^c+O(W^3).$$
The term $N_1^cD_1$ is a connected first-order piece times a first-order vacuum loop. Dividing by $D$ gives
$$\mathcal G=\frac ND=\mathcal G_0+N_1^c+N_2^c+O(W^3),$$
because $\mathcal G_0(1+D_1+D_2)/D=\mathcal G_0$ and $[N_1^c(1+D_1)+N_2^c]/(1+D_1+\cdots)=N_1^c+N_2^c+O(W^3)$. Only connected diagrams remain. The all-orders version is the combinatorial argument of Eqs. (13.19)-(13.20).

questions.prompt: Book Exercise 13.3 (homework). For the Anderson model of Eqs. (9.23)-(9.26), derive the mean-field Dyson equation diagrammatically. Show that $\mathcal G_{d\sigma}(ik_n)=\dfrac{1}{ik_n-(\varepsilon_d-\mu)-U\langle n_{\bar\sigma}\rangle-\Sigma_{\rm hyb}(ik_n)}$, with $\Sigma_{\rm hyb}(ik_n)=\sum_k |t_k|^2/(ik_n-\xi_k)$, $\xi_k=\varepsilon_k-\mu$.
questions.solution:
1. The hybridization vertices $t_k$ connect the dot line to the lead line. Two such vertices, with the lead propagator between them, form the hybridization self-energy $\Sigma_{\rm hyb}(ik_n)=\sum_k |t_k|^2\,\mathcal G_0(k,ik_n)=\sum_k |t_k|^2/(ik_n-\xi_k)$.
2. The term $Un_{d\uparrow}n_{d\downarrow}$ in mean field gives a constant shift $U\langle n_{\bar\sigma}\rangle$ of the dot level $\varepsilon_d-\mu$. It has no internal momentum and adds to the self-energy as a constant.
3. Summing the geometric series of Dyson's equation (13.29) gives the stated $\mathcal G_{d\sigma}$. This is the diagrammatic version of Eqs. (9.37)-(9.38).
